# CAD-to-CAD Helps Michigan PSAPs Manage Storm Call Surge


October 09, 2026


by Jillian Donley


##


One storm. Thousands of calls. A network of connected computer aided dispatch (CAD) systems.


A major holiday weekend went from routine to chaotic when an unexpected storm swept through southern Michigan the evening of July 3, driving emergency call volumes into the thousands across Lenawee and Jackson counties.


**Call volumes in Lenawee County surged from an average of just 5.5 calls an hour to 1,509 calls in a single hour, more than 270 times the county's typical hourly volume that day.**


“That day, we averaged about five and a half 911 calls an hour up until 5 p.m., with our max being 11,” Lenawee County 911 Director Lt. Chris Hudson said. “In the 5 to 6 p.m. hour, we had 1,509 calls. And from the 6 to 7 p.m. hour, we had 628 additional calls.”


In neighboring Jackson County, call surges reached similar levels.


“We were peaking at that 1,500 call volume mark during the duration of the storm as well,” Jackson County 911 Deputy Director Mallory Fugate recalled. “And I think before that total for the day, we had less than 300 calls for the whole rest of the day beforehand.”


As a rollover answering PSAP for Hillsdale and Jackson counties, Lenawee County dispatchers found themselves handling calls from neighboring jurisdictions while simultaneously managing their own surge in emergency calls.


“For us, it was hectic. It was busy,” Hudson said. “We wouldn't have been able to make any calls out to any of the surrounding counties because they would have either kept ringing or rolled over back to us.”


Amid the call surges, CAD-to-CAD connectivity enabled dispatchers in the two neighboring counties to share critical incident information without overloading phone lines or adding extra steps to an already demanding workflow.


**The technology proved especially valuable when emergency incidents began crossing jurisdictions.**


At 5:42 p.m., Lenawee County received a call reporting smoke and a burning smell coming from a residence in Jackson County. A second call confirmed the sight of smoke.


“With this incident, we were able to have the dispatchers hit the CAD-to-CAD button and send the call over to Jackson in a quick radio transmission to let them know that we just sent them a structure fire,” Hudson said.


Before implementing CAD-to-CAD, dispatchers in both counties primarily relied on direct phone calls to relay incident information. An alternative option was Michigan's Law Enforcement Information Network (LEIN) messaging system, but that approach depended on the receiving agency’s ability to notice and access the message.


During a major regional event, both methods could create additional challenges and delays when communications centers are already operating under extraordinary call volumes.


These challenges were highlighted when, amid extraordinary call volumes on July 3, Jackson County experienced a network outage that disrupted access to its CAD and LEIN systems for approximately 18 hours.


"Even if they had tried to send a LEIN message, it wouldn't have ever made it to us, and they wouldn't have had any indication that it hadn't,” Fugate explained.


Beyond enabling faster information sharing, CAD-to-CAD helps dispatchers eliminate duplicate work and maintain a complete record of incident details as calls move between agencies.


“CAD-to-CAD is our primary way of sending calls back and forth,” Hudson said. “It cuts down on the dispatcher's time to re-enter the whole call. It comes over and we have that call with all the information that we need.”


Because the CAD systems are connected, details entered by one agency are automatically embedded within the transferred call record. **Rather than gathering or re-entering details a second time, the neighboring dispatchers receive the information they need to begin coordinating a response immediately.**


“If Lenawee County's dispatchers don't remember to ask what the nearest cross street or a major intersection is, or if it's in a subdivision or something along those lines, all that information is already embedded in the call,” Fugate shared.


“They don't have to remember what type of questions they still have to get from us. It cuts back on that redundancy because if they do forget to ask those questions for either center, then they have to make those calls, get the correct information. And that’s still time they’re not saving before CAD-to-CAD.”


Later that evening, the two counties leveraged their CAD-to-CAD connectivity again when Jackson County requested mutual aid from Lenawee County for an additional structure fire response.


“All of our maps are built out, all of our information is built out to transfer over,” Fugate said.


“The information that our units were already telling us is already passed on to the Lenawee units,” she added. “They're able to read everything that we've already put into the call without having to ask any questions.”


For Lenawee and Jackson counties, the July 3 storm demonstrated the value of seamless information sharing during an emergency.


As call volumes surged and incidents crossed county lines, **connected CAD systems helped ensure critical information moved with them at the speed of the emergency.**
